body.objective: Students will be able to layer clothing for the weather.
body.iCan: I can layer clothing for the weather.
successCriteria: I can explain the three-layer system
I can choose clothing for different Alberta weather
I can recognize and prevent cold and heat injuries
body.hook: In Alberta, the weather can change from sunny to snowing in an afternoon, and in winter, temperatures can fall below −30°C. Outdoor people have a saying: "There's no bad weather, only bad clothing." Knowing how to dress in layers keeps you warm, dry and safe.

vocabulary.definition: The layer next to the skin that moves sweat away.
The middle layer that traps body heat, such as fleece or wool.
The outer layer that blocks wind and water.
How cold it feels on skin when wind is combined with low temperature.
A dangerous drop in body temperature.
Freezing of skin and the tissue underneath.

study.title: Dress for the Weather
study.question: How do I dress to stay safe and comfortable outdoors?
study.passage:
The three-layer system:
1. Base layer: wicks sweat away from skin. Synthetic fabrics or merino wool, not cotton.
2. Insulating layer: traps warm air. Fleece, wool or a down or synthetic jacket.
3. Shell layer: blocks wind, rain and snow.
Plus: a hat (much heat is lost from the head and neck), mitts or gloves, warm socks and waterproof boots.
Why not cotton? Cotton soaks up sweat and water and dries slowly, so it pulls heat away from the body. Outdoor educators say "cotton kills" in cold, wet conditions.
Warning signs:
• Frostbite: skin turns white or grey and feels numb or waxy, often on fingers, toes, ears and nose. Warm gently; don't rub.
• Hypothermia: shivering, clumsy hands, slurred speech, confusion. Get the person somewhere warm and dry and get help.
• Heat exhaustion (summer): heavy sweating, headache, dizziness. Move to shade, drink water.
Activity: Each group gets a weather card: (A) −15°C, wind 20 km/h, sunny; (B) 8°C, rain, windy; (C) 28°C, sunny, a 3-hour hike; (D) −2°C, wet snow. Choose clothing from a pile of real items (or picture cards) and explain each choice. Then go outside for 20 minutes and check how you feel.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; safety information summarized from Environment and Climate Change Canada and Alberta Health Services guidance.
steps: Discuss why cotton is risky in cold and wet weather
Go outside and reflect on comfort
discussion: Why does the base layer matter even in cold weather?
What did your group choose for the rainy 8°C card, and why?
What are early signs of hypothermia?
How did you feel after 20 minutes outside?
study.product: Make a packing list for a winter half-day outing in your area, labelling each item's layer or purpose and including one cold-injury warning sign to watch for.

examples.title: Cotton
examples.problem: Why is a cotton hoodie a poor base layer in winter?
examples.answer: It soaks up sweat and makes you cold

examples.title: Wind chill
examples.problem: It's −10°C with strong wind. Why does it feel colder?
examples.answer: Wind chill makes exposed skin lose heat faster
examples.explore: How do you protect your face?

examples.title: Frostbite
examples.problem: A friend's cheek looks white and waxy. What do you do?
examples.answer: Cover and warm the area gently and get them indoors

practice.q: What does a base layer do?
practice.a: Moves sweat away from the skin.

practice.q: What does a shell layer do?

practice.a: A dangerous drop in body temperature.
Freezing of skin and tissue underneath.

practice.q: Why is cotton risky in cold, wet weather?
practice.a: It holds water and dries slowly, pulling heat away.
Fleece and wool (also down, synthetic fill).
How cold it feels when wind combines with low temperature.
Shivering and confusion (also slurred speech, clumsy hands).

practice.q: What should you do for frostbite?
Name a sign of heat exhaustion.
Why do you remove layers when working hard outdoors?
practice.a: To avoid sweating, which makes you cold later.

practice.q: Why does a hat matter in winter?
practice.a: A lot of body heat is lost from the head and neck.

practice.q: How should clothing change for card C (28°C hike)?
practice.a: Light, breathable layers, a sun hat, sunscreen and water.

practice.q: Why check on friends regularly in the cold?
practice.a: People with hypothermia may not notice their own symptoms.

misconceptions: Thinking one thick jacket is better than layers
Thinking cotton is fine for winter activities
